why_how.text: Defensive driving rests on eight habits that keep you ready for others' mistakes.
Distraction causes crashes, injuries, deaths and damage, and it includes mental drift.

scenario.text: Mia approaches an intersection where a side road has a stop sign.

reasoning.text: Defensive drivers assume side-road drivers will blow through stop and yield signs.

result.text: Mia covers her brake and watches the side-road driver until she is past.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking distraction only means looking at a phone.

correction.text: Distraction strikes through mental drift as surely as eyes or hands off the task.

memory_support.text: Hands on, eyes far, mind on the road.

prompt.text: Which defensive habit covers phones and similar devices?

rationale.text: It is one of the eight habits, alongside looking ahead, correct speed, signaling, space, belts, sober driving and a sound vehicle.

narration.text: This chapter is about defensive driving, which means driving to avoid crashes, including the ones other people's mistakes could cause. The manual builds it on eight habits, and the rest of the chapter expands on each one: aggression and road rage, speed and following distance, seat belts and child restraints, work zones and roundabouts, fatigue and devices, and keeping the vehicle sound. This first lesson introduces the eight habits, then covers how to sit and scan, and what distraction really means. Together they set the foundation for everything that follows in the chapter.

lines.text: Prepare and look ahead; correct speed.
Signal; allow space; wear the belt.
Stay rested and sober; sound vehicle; no devices.

narration.text: The manual lists eight defensive habits. Prepare and look ahead. Hold a correct speed. Signal your turns and lane changes. Allow space around your vehicle. Wear your seat belt. Do not drive when tired, medicated or after drinking. Keep your vehicle in sound condition. And keep handheld devices put away. Each habit protects you in a different way, and together they give you time and room to react when something goes wrong. The rest of this chapter takes these habits one by one, so treat this list as a map of everything the defensive driving chapter will cover.

lines.text: Sit upright; both hands on the wheel.
Look far ahead; check mirrors often.
Expect drivers to run their signs.

narration.text: Sit upright and grip the wheel with both hands, because slouching or steering with one hand is dangerous. Look far down the road, past the road just in front of you and past the car ahead. Move your eyes and check your mirrors every few seconds. And assume that drivers on side roads may drive straight through their stop or yield signs. So defensive driving starts with your body and your eyes: a steady position, a wide view of the road, and the expectation that other drivers will sometimes make mistakes you need to be ready for, even when you have the right-of-way.

Distraction is anything that takes your attention away from driving, and it can cause crashes, injuries, deaths and damage. It happens when your mind drifts, just as surely as when your eyes or hands leave the task. So put away phones and stop texting, avoid arguments and eating while driving, restrain children properly, and keep pets in a carrier. You are responsible for operating the vehicle safely, whatever is happening inside it. Settle these things before you start moving, so that once you are on the road, your full attention can stay on driving.

lines.text: Phones are not the only distraction.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think distraction means only phones and screens. The manual says distraction strikes through mental drift as surely as eyes or hands off the task. So a driver lost in thought, or caught up in an argument with a passenger, is distracted even with both hands on the wheel and eyes facing forward. The fix is the same as for any distraction: remove what you can before you drive, and bring your attention back to the road whenever you notice it wandering. Safe operation of the vehicle is always the driver's responsibility.

Here is a quick check: which of the eight defensive habits covers phones and similar devices? Work it out before reading on. The answer is keeping handheld devices put away. The other habits are preparing and looking ahead, holding a correct speed, signaling turns and lane changes, allowing space, wearing the belt, avoiding driving when tired, medicated or drinking, and keeping the vehicle sound. Remember too that distraction is broader than devices: it includes mental drift, arguments, eating, unrestrained children and loose pets, all of which take attention away from driving.

To close, defensive driving rests on eight habits: prepare and look ahead, hold a correct speed, signal turns and lane changes, allow space, wear the belt, avoid driving tired, medicated or after drinking, keep the vehicle sound, and keep handheld devices put away. Sit upright with both hands on the wheel, look far down the road past the car ahead, check your mirrors every few seconds, and expect side-road drivers to run their signs. Distraction is anything that takes your attention, including your own wandering thoughts, so settle phones, food, arguments, children and pets before you drive. Next comes aggressive driving.

why_how.text: Aggressive driving breaks traffic laws and puts everyone at risk.
Road rage turns aggression into criminal acts with serious penalties.

scenario.text: An angry driver tailgates Leo and then follows him after he changes lanes.

reasoning.text: The confronted driver skips eye contact, stays calm, and drives to a police station without stopping if followed.

result.text: Leo stays calm, avoids eye contact, and drives to a police station.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking road rage is just a stronger form of aggressive driving with the same penalties.

correction.text: Aggressive driving breaks traffic laws while road rage breaks criminal laws, once the driver means harm or violence.

memory_support.text: Aggression breaks traffic law; rage breaks criminal law.

prompt.text: Someone follows you after an angry exchange on the road. What should you do?

answer.text: Drive to a police station without stopping.

rationale.text: Stay calm, avoid eye contact, never race, and call in a description, location, plate and direction.

narration.text: This lesson covers aggressive driving and road rage. The manual describes the behaviors that make up aggressive driving, how to respond when another driver is aggressive toward you, and how to avoid becoming an aggressive driver yourself. Then it defines road rage, explains how it differs from aggressive driving, lists the acts that count as road rage, and sets out what it costs the person who gives in to it. The key distinction is that aggressive driving is a traffic matter, while road rage is a crime. We will come back to that line several times.

lines.text: Running signs, signals and school buses.

narration.text: Aggressive driving includes speeding into tailgating, darting lane changes without signaling, passing on the shoulder or unpaved edge, bullying slower road users, running stop signs, signals and stopped school buses, drifting into the left side of the road, and impaired or reckless driving. When an aggressive driver goes further and tries to hurt another driver, it crosses into road rage. So aggressive driving is a pattern of dangerous habits that break traffic safety laws, and it puts everyone around the driver at risk, even before it ever turns into an intention to harm someone.

lines.text: Followed? Drive to a police station.

narration.text: If another driver is aggressive toward you, do not make eye contact. Stay calm and get away safely. Never race the other driver or try to defend your lane. Make sure everyone in your car is belted, and ignore taunts. Call the police with a description of the vehicle, the location, the plate number and the direction it was heading. If you are followed, drive to a police station without stopping. And if the aggressive driver causes a crash, wait at a safe distance and tell the police what happened. The goal is to remove yourself from the situation, not to win it.

To avoid becoming an aggressive driver yourself, give yourself plenty of travel time and travel off-peak when you can. If you will be late, call ahead to relieve the pressure. Start out calm, rested and sober, keep the car's interior soothing, and keep a relaxed posture. Be courteous and forgive other drivers' mistakes, refuse to retaliate, and yield the right-of-way when it helps. The manual's reasoning is simple: a brief wait is better than twisted metal. So most aggression can be prevented before the drive starts, through planning and a calm frame of mind.

Road rage is angry, hostile driving that boils over into violent criminal acts, including provoking and intimidating other people. It differs from aggressive driving because road rage is a crime, while aggressive driving is a traffic violation. Road rage can take hold of anyone, and it can bring fines, jail, probation, and suspension or revocation of the license. Road rage acts include shouting, horn use, obscene gestures and threats, cutting off, tailgating, blocking, chasing, running others off the road and ramming, and getting out of the vehicle to threaten, assault or injure someone.

lines.text: The line is intent to harm.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People think road rage is just aggressive driving turned up a notch, with the same kind of penalty. The manual draws a sharp line. Aggressive driving breaks traffic safety laws, while road rage breaks criminal laws, so the same tailgate or chase counts as a violation until the driver means harm or violence. So the act alone does not decide it; the intent does. A driver who tailgates out of impatience has committed a traffic violation. A driver who tailgates to frighten or hurt someone has crossed into road rage, a crime with criminal penalties.

Here is a quick check: after an angry exchange on the road, another driver starts following you. What should you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to drive to a police station without stopping. Along the way, stay calm, avoid eye contact, never race, keep everyone belted, ignore taunts, and call the police with a description, the location, the plate number and the direction of travel. And remember the line between the two behaviors: aggressive driving is a traffic violation, but once a driver means harm or violence, it becomes road rage, which is a crime.

To wrap up, aggressive driving includes speeding into tailgating, darting unsignaled lane changes, shoulder passing, bullying slower users and running signs, signals and stopped school buses, and it becomes road rage when a driver tries to hurt someone. If confronted, avoid eye contact, stay calm, get away safely, never race, call in the details, and drive to a police station if followed. Prevent your own aggression with time, calm and forgiveness. Road rage is criminal, brings fines, jail and license loss, and costs the angry driver health, judgment, crashes, jobs and family. Next come speed and following distance.

why_how.text: Speed limits are maximums, and conditions can make them unsafe.
Tailgating causes rear-end crashes, so drivers keep a following cushion.

scenario.text: Ana is driving on an expressway in thick fog with a posted limit of fifty-five.

reasoning.text: The manual preaches below-limit speeds on slick or fogged expressways, where even fifty can earn a ticket for unreasonable speed.

result.text: Ana slows well below the limit and keeps a longer gap.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can never be ticketed for driving below the posted limit.

correction.text: Either default limit still punishes unreasonable speed when fog or slick pavement demands less.

memory_support.text: Fifty-five rural, twenty-five city, two seconds behind.

prompt.text: How much following distance should you keep behind a large truck?

rationale.text: The normal cushion is two seconds, but trucks and bad weather demand three or four.

narration.text: This lesson covers two of the defensive habits: holding a correct speed and allowing space. The manual sets out the default speed limits for unposted roads and for New York City, explains why a posted limit is not always a safe speed, and mentions minimum speeds. It also notes that state law requires approved crash-prevention courses to teach the dangers of road rage. Then it turns to following distance: how to measure it in seconds, when to increase it, how to deal with a driver who is tailgating you, and why you should keep room to the side as well.

lines.text: New York City: twenty-five unless posted.
Slow below the limit when conditions demand.

narration.text: Where no limit is posted, the speed limit is fifty-five miles per hour, and in New York City it is twenty-five unless a sign says otherwise. Speed limits are maximums. On slick or foggy expressways, the manual says to drive below the limit, and even fifty can earn a ticket for unreasonable speed in those conditions. Some roads also post minimum speeds, which must be honored. The manual also notes that state law requires every approved crash-prevention course to teach the dangers of road rage. So the posted number is a ceiling, and conditions can lower the safe speed far below it.

lines.text: Three or four near trucks or in bad weather.

narration.text: The manual says tailgating causes a large share of rear-end crashes, so keep room to stop, and brake early and gently. Keep a cushion of at least two seconds: when the car ahead passes a fixed marker, count one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, and you should not reach the marker before you finish. Near trucks or in bad weather, make it three or four seconds. If someone is tailgating you, change lanes or signal and pull off to let them pass, rather than tapping your brakes. And keep space to the side too, so you have an escape route if you need one.

lines.text: Trucks or bad weather: three or four.
Add space behind trucks and in weather.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Drivers learn the two-second rule and use it everywhere. The manual says the normal cushion counts two seconds, but trucks and bad weather demand three or four. So behind a large truck, or on a wet or icy road, two seconds is not enough. Double-check your count in those situations. A related trap applies to speed: unposted roads cap at fifty-five and New York City defaults to twenty-five, yet either limit still punishes unreasonable speed when fog or slick pavement demands less.

Here is a quick check: you are following a large truck on the highway. How much following distance should you keep? Work it out before reading on. The answer is three or four seconds. The normal cushion is two seconds, counted from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed marker, but trucks and bad weather call for more. If someone tailgates you, change lanes or signal and pull off rather than tapping your brakes. And remember the speed defaults: fifty-five on unposted roads and twenty-five in New York City unless posted, with lower speeds when conditions demand.

lines.text: Two seconds, more for trucks and weather.

narration.text: To close, unposted roads cap at fifty-five miles per hour and New York City at twenty-five unless posted, and both are maximums. On slick or foggy roads, drive below the limit, because even a speed under the limit can be unreasonable, and honor any posted minimum. Keep at least a two-second cushion behind the vehicle ahead, measured from a fixed marker, and stretch it to three or four seconds near trucks or in bad weather. Let tailgaters pass by changing lanes or pulling off with a signal, never by tapping the brakes, and keep room to the side for escape. Next come belts and child seats.

title.text: Belts, child seats and air bags

why_how.text: Seat belts save lives and reduce injuries, and the law requires them.
Children need the right restraint for their age and size.

scenario.text: Raj is driving his six-year-old nephew, who wants to use just the seat belt.

reasoning.text: Children four to seven take approved boosters on lap-shoulder belts, since car belts alone never qualify.

result.text: Raj puts his nephew in an approved booster seat with the lap and shoulder belt.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking air bags make seat belts unnecessary.

correction.text: Air bags work with belts, cushioning head-on crashes, helping control and preventing second hits.

memory_support.text: Seat, then booster, then belt; everyone buckled.

prompt.text: Your friend drives without buckling up. How much is the fine for the driver?

rationale.text: Drivers also pay twenty-five to one hundred dollars plus three points for each unrestrained child under sixteen.

narration.text: This lesson covers seat belts, child restraints and air bags. The manual says belts save lives and reduce injuries, and it explains who must be buckled, how the law is enforced, and the fines for not complying. Then it sets out which restraint children need at each age and size: car seats, booster seats, and seat belts, along with the exemptions. Finally it explains how to sit and set up the car so air bags protect you rather than hurt you. These rules are detailed, so we will compare the child restraint stages side by side before the check at the end.

lines.text: Belts save lives and curb injury.
Adults belted; children in proper restraints.
Officers may stop you for belts alone.

narration.text: Seat belts save lives and reduce injuries in crashes. New York requires adults to wear belts and requires belts, boosters or car seats for children. The law has primary enforcement, which means an officer may stop a vehicle only because someone in it is not belted, and drivers, passengers and visitors can all be ticketed. Unbelted drivers face up to fifty dollars, and unbelted passengers sixteen and older face up to fifty dollars each, one per person. Drivers also pay twenty-five to one hundred dollars plus three points for each unrestrained occupant under sixteen.

lines.text: Rear-facing to age two or the seat's limit.

narration.text: Children under four ride in approved car seats, attached with belts or universal anchors. They ride rear-facing until age two, or until they reach the limits set by the seat's maker, and convertible seats can be used longer than infant carriers. Children aged four to seven ride in approved booster seats with lap and shoulder belts, sized according to the maker's guidance, because the car's belts alone never qualify for that age group. So the first two stages are a car seat for the youngest and a booster for children of four to seven years old.

lines.text: Eight to fifteen: own seat belt.
Fit decides when a booster can stop.

narration.text: Children aged eight to fifteen each use their own seat belt. A restraint is still urged for children under four feet nine inches or one hundred pounds, and children past those marks may use belts from age four if the belt truly fits. Exemptions cover emergency vehicles, vehicles made before nineteen sixty-five, most buses, working rural mail carriers, young passengers in for-hire vehicles, and certified medical conditions. And everyone should stay buckled, because loose bodies fly in a crash. So the belt stage starts at eight, with size and fit adjusting the rule for smaller or larger children.

Here is the trap. Parents often move children to the car's seat belt too early. The manual lays out three stages: seats serve under-fours, rear-facing to age two, boosters serve four-to-sevens, and belts serve eight-to-fifteens, with the height and weight rule letting big young riders use a belt and keeping small older riders in a booster. So a six-year-old needs a booster, not just the belt, and a small nine-year-old may still be better off in a booster. Check the child's age first, then their size and how the belt fits.

lines.text: Sit ten inches back; hands at three and nine.
No rear-facing infant before a live air bag.

narration.text: Set the head rests, lock the doors, and put heavy cargo in the trunk. Air bags work together with belts: they cushion you in head-on crashes, help you keep control, and reduce second impacts inside the car. Sit with about ten inches between your chest and the air bag cover, and hold the wheel at the three and nine o'clock positions. Never put a rear-facing infant seat in the front seat in front of a working passenger air bag. So air bags add protection, but only for occupants who are belted and seated at a safe distance from the air bag.

Here is a quick check: what is the fine for a driver who is not wearing a seat belt? Work it out before reading on. The answer is up to fifty dollars. Unbelted passengers sixteen and older also face up to fifty dollars each, and drivers pay twenty-five to one hundred dollars plus three points for each unrestrained occupant under sixteen. Officers may stop a vehicle for a belt violation alone. And for children, remember the stages: car seats under four, boosters from four to seven, and seat belts from eight to fifteen, adjusted for size and fit.

lines.text: Seat, booster, belt by age and size.
Sit back from the air bag.

narration.text: To close, belts save lives, New York requires belts for adults and proper restraints for children, and officers may stop a vehicle for a belt violation alone. Unbelted drivers and passengers sixteen and older face up to fifty dollars, and drivers pay more plus three points for each unrestrained child under sixteen. Children under four ride in approved car seats, rear-facing to age two, children four to seven in boosters, and children eight to fifteen in belts, adjusted by size. Sit about ten inches from the air bag with hands at three and nine, and never put a rear-facing infant in front of a live air bag.

why_how.text: Work zones bring abrupt changes and doubled speeding fines.
Roundabouts work on yielding at entry and moving counterclockwise.

scenario.text: Dev reaches a roundabout and sees a car already circling from his left.

reasoning.text: Approachers peer left at prioritized circlers and slip through true gaps, since the circle owns priority.

result.text: Dev waits for a gap, then enters and travels counterclockwise.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking speeding fines in a work zone apply only when workers are present.

correction.text: Work zones double speeding fines even with no crew present.

memory_support.text: Yield to enter, priority inside, signal right to leave.

prompt.text: You are about to enter a roundabout. Who has priority?

rationale.text: Entries yield to everything on the left.

narration.text: This lesson covers two road features that ask drivers to change their usual habits. First, work zones, where lanes shift, traffic slows suddenly and workers are close to the road. Second, roundabouts, circular intersections where traffic moves counterclockwise and entering drivers yield to those already circling. The manual explains how to approach, enter, circulate in and leave a roundabout, and how walkers and cyclists use them too. Both topics come down to slowing down and giving way at the right moments. We will finish by comparing who has priority when entering a roundabout and once inside it.

lines.text: Speeding fines double, crew or not.

narration.text: In work zones, speeding fines double, even when no crew is present. Expect sudden slowdowns, shifted lanes and workers close to traffic. Orange diamond signs and flaggers, whose signals count the same as signs, call for slowing down, staying alert and obeying. Smart drivers take another route when they can, merge early, follow the distance signs, and keep a gap of two seconds or more, because rear-end crashes are common in work zones. Stay clear of barriers and work vehicles, and in a moving work zone, stay behind the work until you pass the sign marking its end.

A roundabout moves traffic counterclockwise around a central island, and drivers yield when entering. Roundabouts depend on drivers waiting for a gap, and on low speeds created by curved approaches that turn you before you enter. The manual also sets a speed limit for vehicles circling inside. So a roundabout is designed to keep traffic moving slowly and steadily, without the full stops of a signal. The design does part of the work by bending your path as you come in, which naturally slows you down and helps you judge a gap in the traffic already circling.

lines.text: Follow lane signs; slow for walkers.
Look left; enter only in a true gap.

narration.text: As you approach a roundabout, follow the lane signs and slow down for pedestrians in the crosswalk. Look to your left, because traffic already circling has priority, and enter only when there is a true gap. If traffic queues, leave the crosswalk behind you clear. Cyclists may circulate in the lane with you; share the lane with them and never overtake a bicycle inside the roundabout. So entering is about patience: walkers first, circling traffic next, and then you, once a real gap opens. The manual stresses that the circle owns the priority, not the driver arriving.

lines.text: Wait for an adequate gap to enter.

narration.text: Here is the trap. At a roundabout entry, drivers must slow down, look left, and yield because traffic already in the roundabout has the right-of-way. So at a roundabout, arriving does not give you any right to go. You wait until the traffic circling from your left leaves a gap. Treat the yield sign at the entry as a firm rule: the vehicles already in the circle go first, and you join them only when it is clear.

lines.text: Signal right; yield at the exit crosswalk.
Walkers and riders have their own paths.

narration.text: Once you are in the roundabout, you travel counterclockwise and you have priority. Signal right as you exit, and yield to pedestrians in the exit crosswalk. Pedestrians stay on sidewalks and marked crossings, never crossing to the central island, and they cross one lane at a time using the splitter islands as refuges, keeping their eyes open even when they have priority. Cyclists either ride through with traffic at the circle's pace, signaling right to exit, or get off and walk across like pedestrians. So everyone has a defined path through the roundabout.

Here is a quick check: you are about to enter a roundabout. Who has priority? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the traffic already circling. You look left and wait for a true gap, because the circle owns priority. Once you are inside, the priority is yours, and you signal right to exit and yield to pedestrians in the exit crosswalk. And in a work zone on the way, remember that speeding fines double even when no workers are present, so slow down and merge early.

title.text: Work zones and roundabouts in short

lines.text: Signal right; yield at the exit.

narration.text: To close, speeding fines double in work zones even without a crew, so slow down, obey orange signs and flaggers, merge early and keep two seconds or more of space. Roundabouts move traffic counterclockwise around a central island, with low speeds from curved approaches. Approach slowly, watch for walkers, look left, and enter only in a true gap, because the circle owns priority, and never overtake a cyclist inside. Once inside you have priority; signal right to leave and yield at the exit crosswalk. Walkers cross lane by lane using splitter islands, and cyclists ride with traffic or walk across.

why_how.text: Fatigue impairs driving much like alcohol and drugs.
Handheld calls and texting carry fines, points and license penalties.

scenario.text: Lena has been driving for two hours and keeps yawning.

reasoning.text: Prevention calls for a break every one hundred miles or two hours, and a fading driver parks safely at the first signs and naps.

result.text: Lena pulls into a rest area and takes a short nap.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking opening the window or turning up the radio will keep a drowsy driver awake.

correction.text: The fading driver shuns radio and window tricks and parks safely at the first signs.

memory_support.text: Yawning means park; phones mean penalties.

prompt.text: A driver is convicted for the first time of holding a phone to talk while driving. What is the penalty?

answer.text: Two hundred dollars and five points.

rationale.text: Texting fines rise for later offenses within eighteen months, and junior drivers face suspensions.

narration.text: This lesson covers two dangers that come from inside the driver's seat: fatigue and handheld devices. The manual compares drowsy driving to driving after drinking or using drugs, lists the warning signs and the drivers most at risk, and explains how to prevent fatigue and what to do when it hits. Then it sets out the rules and penalties for making handheld phone calls and for texting while driving, including the extra penalties for junior and probationary drivers. Both dangers are avoidable with planning, which is the theme of this whole defensive driving chapter.

lines.text: Warps judgment, like drink or drugs.

narration.text: Fatigue slows your reactions, dulls your awareness and warps your judgment, leading to crashes much as alcohol and drugs do. Its warning signs include closing eyes, a nodding head, yawning, wandering thoughts, not remembering the last few miles, drifting, tailgating, missing signs, jerking back into your lane, and hitting rumble strips. It strikes most often at people who have not slept, long-distance drivers, night drivers, people on medication or drinking, solo drivers, drivers on monotonous roads, young drivers, shift workers and people with sleep disorders, who should see a doctor.

lines.text: Break every hundred miles or two hours.

narration.text: To prevent fatigue, get enough sleep, bring a companion, and take a break every one hundred miles or two hours. Avoid alcohol and drugs that cause drowsiness, following a pharmacist's advice, and do not drive when ill, exhausted or only just awake. If you start to fade, accept that sleep can come without warning. Opening the window or turning up the radio will not keep you awake. Park somewhere safe at the first signs, take a nap of fifteen to forty-five minutes off the road, and give caffeine about thirty minutes to take effect before driving on.

Here is the trap. Drowsy drivers often try to push on with loud music or cold air. The manual says the fading driver must accept that sleep is unpredictable, avoid radio and window ruses, and park somewhere safe at the first signs of fatigue. So those tricks give a false sense of safety while the danger keeps growing. The real fixes are prevention, with good sleep and regular breaks, and, once fatigue sets in, stopping. A short nap off the road, with caffeine given time to work, is the manual's answer for a driver who is already tired.

lines.text: Handheld call: up to two hundred, five points.

narration.text: Making a handheld phone call carries a fine of up to two hundred dollars and five points for a first offense. You may touch the phone only to start or end a call, emergency calls and uniformed crews on duty are exempt, and hands-free use is always legal. Texting brings a fine of up to two hundred dollars first, up to two hundred fifty second within eighteen months, and up to four hundred fifty for later offenses within eighteen months. Junior and probationary drivers face a one-hundred-twenty-day suspension, and then a year or more if it happens again within six months of getting the license back.

Here is a quick check: what does a first conviction for a handheld phone call cost? Work it out before reading on. The answer is up to two hundred dollars and five points. Texting fines rise with each offense within eighteen months, and junior and probationary drivers lose their license for one hundred twenty days, then a year or more for a repeat within six months of getting it back. Hands-free use is always legal. And remember the fatigue rule: if you start nodding or drifting, park safely and nap, rather than relying on the radio or an open window.

To wrap up, fatigue slows reactions and warps judgment much like alcohol and drugs, and its warning signs include nodding, yawning, lost miles, drifting and missed signs. Prevent it with sleep, a companion, a break every one hundred miles or two hours, and no drowsy-making drugs or alcohol, and when it hits, park safely, nap fifteen to forty-five minutes, and give caffeine thirty minutes. A first handheld call carries up to two hundred dollars and five points, texting fines climb with repeats within eighteen months, and junior and probationary drivers face suspensions. Hands-free use is always legal. Next comes keeping the vehicle sound.

why_how.text: The operator is fully responsible for the vehicle's condition.
Brakes, steering, lights, tires, glass and horn all need regular checks.

scenario.text: Omar's brakes pull to one side after he drives through a deep puddle.

reasoning.text: Pulling brakes want drying with light-pedal runs, then shop care, with instant attention to fading feel.

result.text: Omar presses the brakes lightly to dry them, then has them checked.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a yearly inspection makes the vehicle the inspector's responsibility.

correction.text: Every vehicle needs a yearly inspection, yet operators own roadworthiness absolutely.

memory_support.text: You own the car's condition, every day.

prompt.text: What is the minimum safe tire tread depth?

rationale.text: Check it with the wear bars or the Lincoln-penny test, and look for cuts, bulges and bumps too.

narration.text: This last lesson of the defensive driving chapter covers keeping your vehicle sound, one of the eight defensive habits. The manual says every vehicle on public roads needs a yearly inspection, but that the driver remains fully responsible for its condition between inspections. It then goes through the systems to watch: brakes, steering, lights, tires, glass and wipers, and the horn. It closes the chapter with review questions on everything you have learned. A vehicle in good condition gives you the margin you need when you have to stop, steer or see quickly.

lines.text: Fix faults now; the operator answers.

narration.text: No vehicle may be driven on public roads without a yearly inspection. Beyond that, follow the maker's maintenance guide and get faults fixed right away. Watch your brakes, steering, lights, tires and horn. The manual is firm that the person operating the vehicle is absolutely responsible for its roadworthiness. So the inspection sticker does not move the responsibility to anyone else. If something is wrong with the vehicle on any given day, it is the driver's responsibility to notice it and to have it fixed, rather than waiting for the next inspection to catch the problem.

lines.text: Pulling brakes: dry them, then service.
Steering: little free play; check fluid.

narration.text: If your brakes pull, for example after driving through water, dry them with light pedal pressure, then have them serviced, and get immediate attention if the pedal feel fades. Steering should have very little free play; watch the power steering fluid, and check quickly if you hear a whine. Keep your lights clean, unbroken and properly aimed, so you can see as well as possible at night. So each of these systems gives warning signs before it fails completely, and the defensive driver notices the warnings and acts on them early, before they turn into an emergency on the road.

lines.text: Wear bars or the penny test.

narration.text: Tires need at least two thirty-seconds of an inch of tread, which you can check with the built-in wear bars or with the Lincoln-penny test. Cuts in the cord, bulges and bumps mean the car should not be driven until the tire is replaced, and pressures should match the maker's figures, checked with a gauge. Keep your windows clear with working wipers, defrosters and washer fluid. Use the horn to warn others, not to vent anger, and get it fixed quickly if it fails. These checks take little time and keep the vehicle safe between inspections.

title.text: The sticker is not the guarantee

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think that once the car has passed its yearly inspection, keeping it safe is the inspector's job until next year. The manual says no vehicle may use public roads without a yearly inspection, yet makers guide upkeep, faults should be fixed right away, owners keep watch on brakes, steering, lights, tires and horn, and operators own roadworthiness absolutely. So a sticker on the windshield does not cover a brake that starts pulling next month. If a problem appears between inspections, it is still yours to notice and to fix before you drive on.

Here is a quick check: what is the minimum safe tire tread depth? Work it out before reading on. The answer is two thirty-seconds of an inch, checked with the wear bars or the Lincoln-penny test. Also look for cuts, bulges and bumps, and keep the pressure at the maker's figure, measured with a gauge. Remember the bigger rule: every vehicle needs a yearly inspection, but the operator is absolutely responsible for its condition every day. lines.text: Brakes, steering, lights, tires, glass, horn.

narration.text: To close, every vehicle needs a yearly inspection, but the operator owns its roadworthiness absolutely, following the maker's guide and fixing faults right away. Dry pulling brakes with light pressure and then have them serviced, keep steering free play small, and keep lights clean and aimed. Tires need at least two thirty-seconds of tread, checked by wear bars or the penny test, with cuts and bulges grounding the car. Keep glass clear and the horn working, and use it to warn, not to vent. The chapter's review questions cover scanning, city speed, limits, belts, fatigue, road rage, work zones and roundabouts.
